@C_Barraud's Wednesday Brief is packed with analysis of the Democrats winning control of the House and Senate which, in contrast to conventional thinking, is seeing both bonds and stocks (and gold) higher with the asset taking the biggest hit the dollar.

▪️ Dollar: Bloomberg’s dollar index fell as much as 0.5%, its biggest drop in two months, to its lowest since late September. The Swiss franc, yen and euro all gained.
▪️ Treasuries: the 10-year yield is down 3 basis points to 4.93%. The 5-year fell as much as 9 basis points to 4.67% before pairing some gains.
▪️ Stocks: S&P 500 futures recovered from a 1.4% overnight drop to trade about 0.9% higher, and Nasdaq 100 futures erased a 2.4% slide.
▪️ Gold is up nearly 3% since Tuesday’s close.

Why bonds are rallying: Wellington’s Brij Khurana told Bloomberg divided government has historically been good for Treasuries, since a Democratic Congress limits Trump’s room for more tax cuts and spending that would need more issuance. 
Nedgroup’s David Roberts added a growth angle: Democratic control could slow the AI buildout that has been driving growth and inflation, so the Fed might not need to hike next year.

Why the dollar fell hardest: its 4% rally since early September was built on the AI boom, through money pouring into US tech and AI-driven inflation lifting Fed hike bets. Democrats are talking tougher tech rules and higher taxes on companies and high earners. Crédit Agricole’s David Forrester said the dollar’s “Achilles’ heel” is being exposed. Nomura’s Dominic Bunning added that investors were leaning long the dollar, so there’s room for those bets to unwind.

Vontobel’s Andrew Jackson though noted that blocking new spending doesn’t shrink the existing deficit, so heavy issuance could limit how far long yields fall. Ed Yardeni warned a Democratic sweep could make debt ceiling talks messy, with shutdown risk that could push yields higher (although Republicans may look to get the debt ceiling taken care of in the lame duck session). And dollar bulls have oil: Bloomberg notes the dollar’s gains could resume if Middle East turbulence lifts crude and Fed hike bets.

What to watch: the Treasury’s refunding announcement later this morning, where dealers expect groundwork for possible 2027 cuts to the longest-dated auctions, offset by more bills and shorter notes (Commerzbank expects no coupon changes for now).

In the third-quarter Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS), banks reported that business loan demand weakened for the first time since the second quarter of 2025. But other data doesn’t show businesses borrowing less.

The Fed’s weekly bank lending data shows commercial & industrial (C&I) loans are up 11.3% year-over-year, the fastest since early 2023 (h/t Ed Yardeni), and we know equipment spending surged at a 20.9% annualized rate in third-quarter GDP.

The banks’ own explanation hints at what’s going on: “customer borrowing shifting to more attractive bank or nonbank funding sources.”

Worth noting, the survey’s demand reading has historically led actual C&I loan growth by about three quarters (correlation of 0.64 since 1991), so either loan growth cools into mid-2027 or the survey is off this time.

Interestingly, though, while banks left business loan standards little changed, they tightened standards on every type of loan to the nonbank lenders (nondepository financial institutions, or NDFIs) that may be taking their business:

▪️ Private credit (business credit intermediaries): a net 22% of banks tightened, while a net 10.7% saw stronger demand from them
▪️ Private equity funds: 15.4% tightened, demand up 5.4%
▪️ Mortgage and consumer credit intermediaries and other NDFIs: 16.7% to 20.4% tightened
Despite that, bank loans to NDFIs are up 20.3% year-over-year, about the 20% to 22% pace they’ve held all year. Meanwhile, loan-loss reserves are flat at $202 billion while total loans grew 7.9%, so coverage slipped to 1.42% of loans from 1.54% a year ago.

Some other nuggets from the SLOOS report:
▪️ Commercial real estate standards tightened in all three categories for the first time since the third quarter of 2024, with large banks flipping tighter after six straight surveys of easing on construction and multifamily loans
▪️ Mortgage demand weakened in all seven categories, while credit card demand was the strongest since the third quarter of 2022

Something I’d never have guessed, even after years working in influencer marketing:

The correlation between the number of sponsored posts on a creator’s account and influencer engagement is U-shaped.

Engagement is highest for KOLs who either have no sponsored content at all – or have a lot of sponsorships.

Creators in the middle have the lowest engagement.

Sample: 6,869 sponsored Instagram posts from 4,908 influencers; 147,877 sponsored Douyin videos from 1,000 influencers; comment-text analysis across 2,015,022 comments; plus two experiments with 168 Twitter users and 208 Instagram users.

I assume this is related to the creator efficiency zone:

Many ads → brands likely see strong impact, so those creators are probably big and established.

No ads → best for readers + the most loyal community.

Middle → ad efficiency isn’t proven yet, but community trust is already broken.

I have an article on more unexpected insights from academic studies here, enjoy reading.

A world where the situation with Iran does not improve, already historically low crude inventories evaporate, refined products blow up and the ensuing unrelenting inflation pushes the Fed and other central banks from hawkish to very hawkish, ending this cycle, is definitely feasible. 

However, there's a ton of AI doom in the air, last week's deleveraging and the recent crash across momentum assets are historical outliers, post-midterm price action was very positive (it reminded me of a miniature version of Trump's 2016 victory), high-risk earnings are mostly behind us, the front end of the Treasury curve already has two more hikes priced in by March, Brent is at 102, and the blue sweep should reduce war-risk premia (lower odds of Trump going wild in the Middle East - if he did, the Senate could revolt against him, and the odds of a House impeachment turning into a Trump removal would no longer be zero, though still small).

Therefore, I think it is time to go risk-on and bet on historical post-midterm seasonality with a 3 month horizon. I like Mag 7 (ex TSLA, too soon to fade the midterms), solar energy, and I continue to like long bonds as a growth-scare hedge. Among data centers, I like those with no Texas exposure (TeraWulf), as Texas unexpectedly electing a Democrat Governor reshapes the landscape. 

Good luck trading
